title: Lyons Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Lyons wells have a 150-foot median depth, 7 gpm median yield, and estimated finished costs of $15,800-$27,000.
h1: What Lyons Wells Are Like Before You Buy or Build
intro_html:
Lyons sits in mountain terrain where most permitted wells draw from unnamed fractured-bedrock aquifers rather than the Denver Basin. Records within five miles show a wide spread in depth and production, so a nearby well is useful evidence but not a guarantee for your parcel.

The Colorado DWR records include 1,863 permitted wells, with 1,078 recorded as constructed. Only 430 report a pump yield and 63 report a static water level. That missing information matters when you are comparing lots, reviewing a seller’s well, or budgeting a new well.

sections.heading: Lyons well depth follows fractured mountain rock
sections.html:
The median reported well depth near Lyons is 150 feet. The middle half runs from 34 to 405 feet, and the 90th percentile is 600 feet. The deepest well in the records reaches 1,630 feet.

Depth is not evenly distributed. Forty-four percent of wells are under 100 feet, 19% are 100-300 feet, 25% are 300-600 feet, and 13% are 600 feet or deeper. That spread is typical of fractured granite and gneiss: a short distance can change where the drill finds usable fractures.

For a drilling bid, the 150-foot median is only a starting point. A contractor needs to allow for harder ground, casing and grout, access, and the possibility that the hole must go substantially deeper than a nearby shallow well.

sections.heading: Most Lyons wells make usable household volumes
sections.html:
Among wells reporting pump yield, the median is 7.0 gallons per minute. The middle half produces 5.0 to 10.0 gallons per minute. Seventy-three percent fall in the 5-15 gpm range, while 11% report more than 15 gpm.

Low production is possible but not the dominant result: 4% report under 1 gpm and 11% report 1-5 gpm. A buyer should still ask for the actual well report, pump test, storage capacity, and recovery information. A 7.0 gpm median describes the local record; it does not promise that a new hole will hit that rate.

Most permitted use is domestic or household use, at 67%. Stock use is 5% and irrigation is 2%, so a planned larger outdoor demand needs separate review of the permit and water rights.

sections.heading: Recorded water levels vary across Lyons
sections.html:
The median static water level is 20 feet below the surface, with the middle half from 10 to 126 feet. Static level means the water level when the well is not being pumped; it is not the same as well depth or available yield.

The decade comparison does not show a simple dropping water table in these records. The median measured level was 46 feet below surface in the 2010s and 17 feet in the 2020s. Those measurements come from only 63 wells overall, and differences in location, season, construction, and measurement method can affect the comparison.

Before buying, have the current well condition and water level checked rather than treating the area median as a site-specific measurement. In mountain bedrock, fractures can produce sharp local differences.

sections.heading: Lyons permit history shows long local drilling activity
sections.html:
Permit records show drilling activity from the 1950s through the 2020s, with the newest permit issued in 2025. The largest decade totals are 425 permits in the 1990s, 346 in the 1980s, and 274 in the 1970s. There are also 98 permits in the 2020s.

The most active named drillers in these records are Ingram Drilling Inc., also listed as Ingram, Stephen E., with 234 records; Ground Water Systems Inc, also listed as Wilson, Richard R., with 178; and Authorized (Pe, Pg), with 163. These counts describe permit records, not current availability or a recommendation.

Colorado DWR permit history can help confirm the permitted use, construction details, and reported production for an existing well. Have the permit number and well construction report reviewed before relying on a seller’s description.

sections.heading: Budgeting a new well near Lyons
sections.html:
Local ground conditions are fractured mountain bedrock, described in the cost model as granite and gneiss. The drilling rate is estimated at $65-$100 per foot. At the 150-foot median depth, the drilled hole works out to about $9,800-$15,000.

A finished well, including the pump, tank, trenching, and electrical, is estimated at $15,800-$27,000. Those figures are planning numbers, not a fixed bid. Difficult access, extra casing or grout, deeper drilling, water testing, power distance, and site conditions can change the total.

Ask a driller to separate the per-foot drilling allowance from pump equipment and site work. On a steep or rocky lot near Lyons, driveway access and trenching can be as important to the final price as the hole itself.

sections.heading: What to investigate before relying on a Lyons well
sections.html:
Low yield and a dry hole are the main physical uncertainties in fractured mountain rock. The local records include 4% of reported yields under 1 gpm, and the depth range extends to 1,630 feet. A neighboring well can show local conditions, but it cannot guarantee the result on a different fracture system.

Water quality also deserves independent testing. Mapped environmental information within about 10 miles includes 60 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 258 historic mine features, and 15 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Those map layers do not establish contamination at a particular well; they are reasons to test and review site history.

Check septic setbacks, drainfield space, access for a rig, electrical service, and the proposed building location. Confirm the DWR permit allows the intended household, stock, or irrigation use before closing.

sections.heading: A practical plan for a Lyons lot
sections.html:
Start with the DWR permit and construction report for any existing well. Confirm depth, casing, pump information, permitted use, and reported yield. If the well has a low or missing production record, arrange a current flow and recovery evaluation before assigning it much value.

For a vacant parcel, compare several nearby records in Lyons, Altona, Jamestown, Longmont, Lazy Acres, and Niwot, while remembering that fractured bedrock can change quickly. Get a written drilling proposal that explains what happens if the hole must go deeper or does not produce enough water.

Finally, coordinate the well, septic system, driveway, and house pad before construction. If the proposed use exceeds an exempt household-use well’s limits or the basin is over-appropriated, Colorado water-rights and augmentation requirements may affect the project.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Lyons, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported depth near Lyons is 150 feet. The middle half of wells runs from 34 to 405 feet, but 13% are 600 feet or deeper and the deepest record is 1,630 feet. Because the area is fractured mountain bedrock, a nearby well does not reliably predict the depth on another parcel.

faq.q: What does a well cost to drill in Lyons?
faq.a: The local cost model uses $65-$100 per foot in granite and gneiss. At the 150-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at $9,800-$15,000. A finished well with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $15,800-$27,000. Access, depth, casing, power, and site work can change a bid.

faq.q: How much water do Lyons wells produce?
faq.a: Reported pump yields have a 7.0 gpm median, with the middle half from 5.0 to 10.0 gpm. Seventy-three percent are in the 5-15 gpm range. However, 4% report under 1 gpm and 11% report 1-5 gpm, so review the actual well report and pump test rather than relying only on the local median.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Lyons?
faq.a: The well records do not establish drinking-water safety. Within about 10 miles, mapped information includes 60 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 258 historic mine features, and 15 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. These maps do not prove a problem at your well, but they support having the water tested and reviewing local site history before drinking it.

faq.q: Is the water table dropping near Lyons?
faq.a: The available decade medians do not show a simple decline. Reported static water level was 46 feet below surface in the 2010s and 17 feet in the 2020s. Only 63 wells report a static water level, and location, season, construction, and measurement conditions can differ. Get a current measurement for the specific well before drawing a trend conclusion.
